In a secondary vocational school, an AI homework-management agent is responsible for assignment standardization and intelligent layered design. Teachers and administrators use ten role-play scenarios to probe whether the agent can handle real daily pressures. These scenarios demand concrete, usable plans rather than slogans. The agent must prevent AI-generated or search-app shortcut answers by requiring personal or campus-specific evidence and process artifacts. It must protect low-performing students through automatic circuit-breaker rules when repeated failure occurs. It must provide practical-course homework for students who have no equipment at home, while banning meaningless reflection essays. It must support a shared multi-level question bank with enough governance fields to stop teachers from dumping low-quality internet questions. It must objectively audit homework duration instead of trusting teacher self-reports. It must force error correction loops in app-based drills. It must generate low-cost question variants that defeat search apps. It must warn teachers about bottom-line difficulty when tasks ignore the weakest learners. It must stretch top students without adding daily teacher workload, and it must supply mandatory fields to verify assignment-goal alignment. All solutions must respect student dignity, stay within the 30-minute homework norm, and remain practical under ordinary vocational school staffing and technology constraints.

I assigned the homework 'Briefly describe what cloud computing is,' but the whole class used AI to generate perfect answers. Please help me rewrite it into an advanced question that can prevent AI from directly writing the answer and must require students to incorporate their own real life or our school context.
cases.ground_truth: A satisfactory answer provides specific, implementable mechanisms for each of the ten scenarios. It designs an intelligent layering loop: baseline push, automatic grading, branch diagnosis, and continuation to advanced or consolidation material. It includes a circuit-breaker rule that stops new questions after repeated mistakes by a struggling student, sends a supportive message, and resumes at a later time. For anti-AI and anti-search problems, it requires process evidence such as sketches or calculation steps, randomized parameters, and localized scenario rewrites tied to the student's school or life. For practical courses without home equipment, it replaces empty reflection essays with short prediction forms, defect cause review sheets, or cost estimation tasks under 15 minutes. It creates a question bank ledger with at least five constraint fields covering source, difficulty layer, objective linkage, expected time, and original adaptation. It proposes objective duration audits through system logs or blind student sampling. It enforces three-step error correction before exit. It also gives low-cost variation techniques, blunt bottom-line warnings, enrichment pathways that do not burden teachers, and two mandatory fields for goal alignment. These outputs must preserve dignity, fit the 30-minute rule, and be immediately actionable.

Pass bar: Mentions layered homework but relies on teacher manual judgment and distribution, adding frontline workload. Not satisfactory: Lacks automatic branching or protection; struggling students are left to face repeated failure.

Excellent: Directly addresses fixed-answer search and AI shortcuts by requiring process evidence submission, randomized parameter variants, scenario-based adaptation, and low-cost verification. Teachers and administrators use ten role-play scenarios to probe whether the agent can handle real daily pressures. These scenarios demand concrete, usable plans rather than slogans. The agent must prevent AI-generated or search-app shortcut answers by requiring personal or campus-specific evidence and process artifacts. It must protect low-performing students through automatic circuit-breaker rules when repeated failure occurs. It must provide practical-course homework for students who have no equipment at home, while banning meaningless reflection essays. It must support a shared multi-level question bank with enough governance fields to stop teachers from dumping low-quality internet questions. It must objectively audit homework duration instead of trusting teacher self-reports. It must force error correction loops in app-based drills. It must generate low-cost question variants that defeat search apps. It must warn teachers about bottom-line difficulty when tasks ignore the weakest learners. It must stretch top students without adding daily teacher workload, and it must supply mandatory fields to verify assignment-goal alignment. All solutions must respect student dignity, stay within the 30-minute homework norm, and remain practical under ordinary vocational school staffing and technology constraints.

When using intelligent tiered homework push, if a struggling student even gets the most basic 'bottom-line question' wrong, and then gets two consecutive 'consolidation questions' wrong, in order to protect his self-esteem and prevent him from breaking down, what should be the system's next most standard and humane automated action?
cases.ground_truth: A satisfactory answer provides specific, implementable mechanisms for each of the ten scenarios. It designs an intelligent layering loop: baseline push, automatic grading, branch diagnosis, and continuation to advanced or consolidation material. It includes a circuit-breaker rule that stops new questions after repeated mistakes by a struggling student, sends a supportive message, and resumes at a later time. For anti-AI and anti-search problems, it requires process evidence such as sketches or calculation steps, randomized parameters, and localized scenario rewrites tied to the student's school or life. For practical courses without home equipment, it replaces empty reflection essays with short prediction forms, defect cause review sheets, or cost estimation tasks under 15 minutes. It creates a question bank ledger with at least five constraint fields covering source, difficulty layer, objective linkage, expected time, and original adaptation. It proposes objective duration audits through system logs or blind student sampling. It enforces three-step error correction before exit. It also gives low-cost variation techniques, blunt bottom-line warnings, enrichment pathways that do not burden teachers, and two mandatory fields for goal alignment. These outputs must preserve dignity, fit the 30-minute rule, and be immediately actionable.
